notes.summary: The Rab band is not one band: wherever it isn't saturated it splits into three main sub-bands about 4-5% apart in size (upper, middle and lower), with weaker ones below. Without the defect the middle one dominates; with the defect all three grow, but the upper and lower ones far more than the middle, so the mix shifts. This holds on the frozen-blood, RBC-lysis and drop-out gels, so confidence that the defect changes the mix is moderate to high; which Rabs the sub-bands are is unknown, and matching them between gels is by pattern, not by exact size.
findings: Frozen blood (24/09/26), 1 in 10: the defect lane has about 39x the no-defect lane's upper sub-band, 26x its lower and 8x its middle, with or without protease inhibitor.
RBC lysis (19/08/26), 3x lysis: per µg of lysate, about 16x (upper), 10x (lower) and 2x (middle) with the defect. The same order as on the frozen-blood gel.
Reaction drop-outs (04/11/26): the no-defect full reaction is mostly middle (35%); the defect lanes that could be measured (without REP1, without RabGGTase II) are mostly lower and upper.
If each sub-band is a different Rab, or a group of Rabs, the defect leaves some of them unprenylated far more than others: the upper sub-band most, the middle least.
notes.method: Before any fitting, each lane's darkness profile has a slowly varying background taken off (a rolling minimum, then a rolling mean, over about an eighth of the gel's height), and is scaled so a saturated pixel is 1; the fit view shows the profile before and after, with the background that was removed. Each lane's profile between 20.5 and 28.5 kDa is then fitted as a sum of Gaussian peaks plus a small sloping baseline of its own. The peak positions are found once per gel, from the curvature of all its usable lanes, so a shoulder counts as well as a separate peak; each lane's peaks may then shift together by up to about 2% and individually by about 1%, with one width per lane. The area of each peak is its amount; its share is its area over the lane's total. Lanes with a saturated pixel in this region are set aside, since a flat top can't be split, and so are lanes with almost no signal.
caveats: Every saturated lane is set aside, which is most defect lanes at the higher lysate amounts and both reacted lanes on the Strep pull-down gel, so the comparisons use the more dilute lanes.
Sub-bands 4-5% apart sit at the limit of what a 4-20% gel resolves; the split is a model that fits the profiles closely (R² 0.95-1.00), not a direct separation.

On the frozen-blood gel the faint line seen at the middle position in the most dilute lanes of both genotypes may come partly from the reaction mix, which would inflate the middle share in dilute no-defect lanes.
On the serial dilution (18/09/26) the lanes don't line up well enough in this region to say which sub-band is which between lanes, so its sub-bands aren't matched to the other gels.
Identifying the sub-bands needs antibodies against individual Rabs (Rab27a is a candidate in blood) or mass spectrometry of the labelled proteins.

gels.G1: Nothing to split: the two reacted lanes are saturated across the Rab region and the bead eluates have no Rab signal.
gels.G5: Shown as fitted, but not matched: the lanes don't line up well enough here, so sub-band colours on this gel are by position only and don't correspond to the other gels.

notes.reference: Lining lanes up on the ~54 kDa band instead of the ladder: that band comes from the reaction mix, so it is the same protein in every reacted lane, a size marker inside the lane. Measured against it, the three sub-bands sit at about 25.0, 23.9 and 23.0 kDa on the drop-out, frozen-blood and RBC-lysis gels alike (spread about 1.4% across 16 lanes, against about 2% using the ladders), and the frozen-blood gel's 4% offset goes away, which supports matching the sub-bands between gels. The endogenous ~74 kDa band was also tried, but in reacted lanes it is too weak to place precisely and made the spread worse (about 3%).
